stufe_0_frage: What tools does an electronics engineer need?
stufe_1_frage: Why does something oscillate on its own?
stufe_2_frage: How does music travel through the air?
stufe_3_frage: How do you turn a little voltage into more – without heat?
stufe_4_frage: How do you dim AC voltage?
stufe_5_frage: How much power, how much heat?
stufe_6_frage: How do you measure tiny changes?
stufe_7_frage: How does a voltage become a one?
lex_spule_hf: These small coils have only a few turns. They suit fast oscillations. The 220 µH (microhenry) antenna coil and the variable capacitor form the tuned circuit of your radio. There are also 1 mH and 10 mH coils for lower tones.
lex_drossel: A storage choke is a coil of thick wire on a ferrite core. It has 10 mH and only 2 Ω. That is why it can take 0.5 A and hardly gets warm. In a switching converter it stores energy in every cycle and then gives it back.
lex_uebertrager: A transformer has two windings on a ring core. When current flows through one, a magnetic field forms. When it changes, it also makes a voltage in the other one. The dots show where each winding starts. Both are wound the same way round.
lex_led_weiss: A white LED is a blue LED on the inside. A yellow glowing layer turns the blue light into white light. That is why, like the blue one, it needs about 3 volts.
lex_drehkondensator: A variable capacitor has plates that turn into each other. The further they overlap, the larger the capacitance: from 10 to 500 pF (picofarad). Tap it and the knob appears. This is how you tune a tuned circuit.
lex_diode_ge: The germanium diode already conducts from about 0.2 volts. That is why it can pick up very weak transmitters. In the radio it turns the fast oscillation from the antenna back into sound.
lex_kristallhoerer: The crystal earpiece is an earphone without a battery. Inside it sits a thin crystal disc. When a voltage is applied, it bends a little and makes the sound. It needs almost no current. That is why the power of the transmitters is enough for it in a crystal radio.
lex_mwmodul: The MW module is a ready-made medium-wave receiver: tank coil, detector diode and a transistor stage for the loudspeaker. You plug the variable capacitor for tuning in outside at “Tune”. With “Look inside” you can see all the parts with their values.
lex_ukwmodul: The FM module is a ready-made FM receiver with an output stage. The voltage at “Tune” selects the frequency from 87.5 to 108 MHz, the voltage at “Volume” the volume. Between the transmitters it hisses. With “Look inside” you can see the frequency, the reception and the volume.
exp3_1_1_frage: A capacitor stores charge. A coil keeps the current going. What happens when they work together?
exp3_1_1_v1: The voltage swings back and forth and gets smaller.
exp3_1_1_v2: The voltage jumps up once and then stays there.
exp3_1_1_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_1_b1: After every jump, K1 showed a wave that kept getting smaller.
exp3_1_1_b2: K1 only showed jumps, no wave.
exp3_1_1_b3: I couldn’t see anything on the screen.
exp3_1_1_s1: The generator puts out a square wave. Five times a second it jumps up and back down.
exp3_1_1_s2: Connect G through the capacitor C1 to the coil SP1. The other end of the coil goes to 0V.
exp3_1_1_s3: Put probe K1 on C2, between the capacitor and the coil. Look at the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_1_h1: Do you only see jumps? Check that the coil is plugged into C2 and 0V.
exp3_1_1_h2: Is the wave too small or too big? Change the volts per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_1_loesung: After every jump, the voltage at the coil swings back and forth. Each swing is a bit smaller than the one before. After a few swings it has almost gone.
exp3_1_1_erklaerung: At the jump, charge flows into the capacitor. The coil keeps the current going – even when the capacitor is already full. So it charges it too far. Then the charge flows back, and everything starts again. The energy swings back and forth between the capacitor and the coil. Each time, a part of it turns into heat in the coil’s wire. That is why the swing gets smaller. This is called a damped oscillation. A capacitor and a coil together are called a resonant circuit.
exp3_1_1_mehr: In the capacitor the energy sits in the electric field, in the coil in the magnetic field. Without losses the circuit would keep swinging forever. How fast it swings depends on L and C: f = 1 / (2π · √(L · C)). With 1 H and 1 µF that is about 159 Hz.
exp3_1_1_w1: Use a 100 nF capacitor instead of 1 µF. What happens to the wave?
exp3_1_1_w2: Use the 100 mH coil instead of the 1 H coil. Compare the curves.
exp3_1_1_echt: A swing is also a pendulum like this: you push it once. Then it swings back and forth and slowly calms down. There is a resonant circuit in every radio.
exp3_1_2_frage: In the last experiment the circuit swung about 160 times a second. What happens with a smaller coil?
exp3_1_2_v1: With the smaller coil the circuit swings faster.
exp3_1_2_v2: With the smaller coil the circuit swings more slowly.
exp3_1_2_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_2_b1: With the smaller coil the waves were closer together. The frequency went up.
exp3_1_2_b2: With the smaller coil the waves were further apart.
exp3_1_2_s1: Take your circuit from the last experiment. Read the frequency on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_2_s2: Swap the 1 H coil for the 100 mH coil.
exp3_1_2_h1: The frequency is at the top of the screen, to the right of peak-to-peak.
exp3_1_2_h2: Are the waves very narrow? Choose fewer milliseconds per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_2_loesung: With 1 H the circuit swings about 159 times a second, with 100 mH about 500 times. Smaller coil – higher frequency. Bigger coil – lower frequency.
exp3_1_2_erklaerung: A big coil keeps the current going for a long time. A big capacitor takes a long time to fill up. Both make the back and forth slower. With a smaller coil it goes faster. The frequency depends on both: on the inductance L of the coil and on the capacitance C of the capacitor.
exp3_1_2_mehr: The Thomson formula is f = 1 / (2π · √(L · C)). With 100 mH and 1 µF it gives 503 Hz. The coil is ten times smaller, but the frequency is only a bit more than three times higher. That is because the formula has a square root: √10 ≈ 3.16.
exp3_1_2_w1: Use the 1 H coil again, but with a 100 nF capacitor. What do you measure?
exp3_1_2_w2: Put two 1 µF capacitors side by side. How does the frequency change?
exp3_1_2_echt: A guitar works in a similar way: a thick, heavy string swings more slowly and sounds lower than a thin one.
exp3_1_3_frage: In the coil’s wire, a part of the energy turns into heat. What happens if you add a resistor?
exp3_1_3_v2: The swinging gets faster, so it gets higher.
exp3_1_3_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_3_b1: With the resistor there were fewer waves. They got smaller faster.
exp3_1_3_b2: With the resistor the waves were closer together.
exp3_1_3_s1: Take your circuit with the 1 H coil. Count how many waves you see after a jump.
exp3_1_3_s2: Put a 330 Ω resistor between G and the capacitor.
exp3_1_3_h1: The resistor goes into the connection from G to the capacitor. Remove the old wire from G to A1.
exp3_1_3_h2: Can you hardly see any waves? Choose 2 milliseconds per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_1_3_loesung: Without the resistor you see many waves after every jump. With 330 Ω there are only one or two left. The frequency stays almost the same.
exp3_1_3_erklaerung: With every back and forth, the current flows through the resistor. There, a part of the energy turns into heat. The bigger the resistor, the faster the energy is used up. The swinging dies away faster. This is called damping. The frequency hardly changes.
exp3_1_3_mehr: The quality factor Q tells you how strongly a circuit is damped. For a series circuit, Q = √(L / C) / R. R is all the resistances together: the coil with 100 Ω, the generator with 50 Ω and your resistor. With 330 Ω, Q is about 2; without it, about 7. The higher the quality factor, the longer the circuit keeps ringing.
exp3_1_3_w1: Use a 1 kΩ resistor instead of 330 Ω. Does the circuit still swing?
exp3_1_3_w2: Use a 47 Ω resistor. How many waves do you count now?
exp3_1_3_echt: The shock absorbers in a car brake in exactly this way: after a bump, the car shouldn’t keep bouncing for long.
exp3_1_4_frage: A swing goes highest when you push it at the right rhythm. Is that also true for the resonant circuit?
exp3_1_4_v1: At one particular frequency the most current flows.
exp3_1_4_v2: The higher the frequency, the more current flows.
exp3_1_4_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_4_b1: At about 160 Hz the curve at K1 was biggest. Above and below it, it got smaller.
exp3_1_4_b2: The curve kept getting bigger with the frequency.
exp3_1_4_s1: Build a chain: G, 1 µF capacitor, 1 H coil, 100 Ω resistor, 0V.
exp3_1_4_s2: Put probe K1 between the coil and the resistor. The voltage at the resistor shows you how much current flows.
exp3_1_4_s3: The generator puts out a 50 Hz sine wave. Slowly turn the frequency up. Where is the curve biggest?
exp3_1_4_h1: Set the generator to the range 100 to 1000 Hz. Move the slider slowly.
exp3_1_4_h2: You will find the biggest curve near the frequency from the first experiment.
exp3_1_4_loesung: At about 159 Hz the curve is biggest: a little over 0.8 V peak-to-peak. This is also the frequency at which the circuit swings by itself. It is called the resonant frequency.
exp3_1_4_erklaerung: At low frequencies the capacitor holds back the current. At high frequencies the coil holds it back. At the resonant frequency the two cancel each other out exactly. Then only the resistors limit the current. The generator pushes the circuit exactly in time with its own swinging – just like you push a swing.
exp3_1_4_mehr: The AC resistance of the coil is X_L = 2π · f · L, that of the capacitor is X_C = 1 / (2π · f · C). At resonance both are the same size. They work against each other and cancel out. If you set X_L = X_C, you get the Thomson formula again.
exp3_1_4_w1: Swap the coil for the 100 mH coil. Where is the resonance now?
exp3_1_4_w2: Put a second probe on C2, between the capacitor and the coil. How big is the voltage there at resonance? Compare it with the generator.
exp3_1_4_echt: That is why soldiers don’t march in step across a bridge: their rhythm could make the bridge resonate.
exp3_1_5_titel: The parallel circuit as a filter
exp3_1_5_frage: Now the coil and the capacitor sit side by side. A resistor sits in front of them. Which frequencies get through?
exp3_1_5_v1: Only near one frequency does a lot of voltage arrive.
exp3_1_5_v2: All frequencies get through equally well.
exp3_1_5_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_5_b1: At about 160 Hz the curve was big. At low and high frequencies it was small.
exp3_1_5_b2: The curve was the same size at all frequencies.
exp3_1_5_s1: Connect G through a 10 kΩ resistor to C2.
exp3_1_5_s2: Put the 1 µF capacitor and the 1 H coil side by side between C2 and 0V. Put probe K1 on C2.
exp3_1_5_s3: The generator starts at 50 Hz. Slowly turn the frequency up. When is the curve biggest?
exp3_1_5_h1: The coil and the capacitor each have one end on C2 and the other on 0V.
exp3_1_5_h2: You will find the biggest curve near 160 Hz. Move the slider very slowly there.
exp3_1_5_loesung: At about 159 Hz almost 1 V peak-to-peak arrives. At 50 Hz or 500 Hz it is only about 0.07 V. The circuit lets one frequency through and keeps the others away.
exp3_1_5_erklaerung: At low frequencies the coil lets the current flow to 0V almost freely. At high frequencies the capacitor does that. Either way, hardly any voltage is left at C2. At resonance, though, the current swings back and forth between the coil and the capacitor. To the outside, the circuit blocks. Then almost all the voltage arrives. This is how a radio picks one station out of many.
exp3_1_5_mehr: For a series circuit the resistance is smallest at resonance; for a parallel circuit it is biggest. Here it is about 9 kΩ. That is why at 159 Hz the voltage is shared almost half and half between the 10 kΩ resistor and the circuit.
exp3_1_5_w1: Use the 100 mH coil instead of the 1 H coil. Where is the peak now?
exp3_1_5_w2: Use a 1 kΩ resistor instead of 10 kΩ. How does the curve change at resonance and next to it?
exp3_1_5_echt: There is a circuit like this in every radio. When you turn the station dial, you adjust a variable capacitor. That is how you choose which frequency gets through.
exp3_1_6_frage: A radio should keep one station well apart from its neighbours. What happens if the circuit loses extra energy?
exp3_1_6_v1: The peak gets lower and wider. The circuit separates less well.
exp3_1_6_v2: The peak gets higher and narrower.
exp3_1_6_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_6_b1: With the resistor the curve at 159 Hz was smaller. At 140 Hz it was almost as big as at 159 Hz.
exp3_1_6_b2: With the resistor the curve was bigger.
exp3_1_6_s1: Take your circuit from the last experiment. Set 159 Hz. Read the peak-to-peak voltage.
exp3_1_6_s2: Set 140 Hz and read it again. Then set 159 Hz again.
exp3_1_6_s3: Put a 2.2 kΩ resistor next to the circuit: one end on C2, the other on 0V.
exp3_1_6_s4: Measure again at 159 Hz and at 140 Hz. Compare with before.
exp3_1_6_h1: The new resistor is in parallel with the coil and the capacitor. It has one end on C2 and one on 0V.
exp3_1_6_h2: Write the values down. Divide the value at 140 Hz by the value at 159 Hz.
exp3_1_6_loesung: Without the resistor: about 0.95 V at 159 Hz and 0.59 V at 140 Hz. With 2.2 kΩ: about 0.30 V and 0.27 V. The peak is lower and much wider.
exp3_1_6_erklaerung: With every back and forth, the resistor uses up a part of the energy. So the circuit doesn’t swing as strongly. It hardly prefers its own frequency to its neighbours any more. Such a circuit is called wide: it has a low quality factor. A circuit with a high quality factor has a high, narrow peak. It keeps stations well apart.
exp3_1_6_mehr: For a parallel circuit, Q = R / (2π · f · L). R is all the resistances that act in parallel with the circuit: the losses of the coil (here about 9 kΩ), the 10 kΩ resistor in front and your new resistor. Without it, Q is about 5; with 2.2 kΩ, about 1.5. The width of the peak is roughly f / Q.
exp3_1_6_w1: Use a 22 kΩ resistor instead of 2.2 kΩ. Is the peak narrow or wide then?
exp3_1_6_w2: Remove the 2.2 kΩ resistor and find the two frequencies at which the curve is only 0.67 V. How far apart are they?
exp3_1_6_echt: Good radios have circuits with a high quality factor. With cheap receivers you sometimes hear two stations at once – their circuit is too wide.
exp3_1_7_frage: In the first experiment the resonant circuit stopped after every push. Can a transistor keep it swinging forever?
exp3_1_7_v1: With the transistor the circuit keeps swinging. A smaller capacitor makes the tone higher.
exp3_1_7_v2: The circuit dies away again like in the first experiment.
exp3_1_7_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_1_7_b1: The tone stayed. With a smaller C1 it got higher.
exp3_1_7_b2: The tone stopped after a short time.
exp3_1_7_b3: I didn’t hear a tone or see a curve.
exp3_1_7_s1: Transistor T1 keeps the resonant circuit going. There are many parts. Build step by step.
exp3_1_7_s2: The 1 H coil gets its current through the loudspeaker. That way you can hear the circuit.
exp3_1_7_s3: Switch on. Can you hear the tone? Look at the curve at K1.
exp3_1_7_s4: Swap C1 for 470 nF, 220 nF and 100 nF one after the other. How does the tone change?
exp3_1_7_h1: No tone? Check that the main switch is on. The coil must be connected to +9V through the loudspeaker.
exp3_1_7_h2: C1 connects the collector to the emitter, C2 connects the emitter to 0V. Compare with the building plan.
exp3_1_7_loesung: The tone keeps going as long as the battery supplies current. With 1 µF it sounds at about 230 Hz, with 470 nF at about 290 Hz, with 220 nF at about 390 Hz and with 100 nF at about 540 Hz.
exp3_1_7_erklaerung: In the first experiment the circuit lost energy with every back and forth. Now the transistor adds a little energy from the battery in every beat. It gets the beat from the circuit itself: through C1 and C2, part of the swinging goes back to its emitter. This is called feedback. So the circuit keeps swinging. A circuit like this is called an oscillator. Together, C1 and C2 act like a smaller capacitor. If C1 is smaller, the tone gets higher.
exp3_1_7_mehr: This circuit is called a Colpitts oscillator. C1 and C2 are in series. Together they act like C = C1 · C2 / (C1 + C2). With two times 1 µF that is 0.5 µF. The Thomson formula then gives 225 Hz. Volta measures a little more because the transistor is connected to the circuit too. The voltage at the collector even swings above the battery’s 9 V: the coil gives back the energy it has stored.
exp3_1_7_w1: Use a 470 nF capacitor for C2. What happens to the tone?
exp3_1_7_w2: Use the 100 mH coil instead of the 1 H coil. How high does the oscillator sound now?
exp3_1_7_echt: In every radio transmitter an oscillator with a resonant circuit makes the carrier wave – only much faster than this one.
exp3_2_1_frage: A radio station sends music through the air. For that it needs a very fast oscillation. How is the slow tone hidden inside it?
exp3_2_1_v1: The tone makes the fast oscillation bigger and smaller in turn.
exp3_2_1_v2: The tone and the fast oscillation run separately, side by side.
exp3_2_1_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_2_1_b1: The peaks of the fast curve rose and fell in time with the tone. Together they formed a slow wave.
exp3_2_1_b2: The curve stayed the same height everywhere.
exp3_2_1_s1: Put a 10 kΩ resistor from A1 to A2. Connect G to A1 and A2 to 0V.
exp3_2_1_s2: Put probe K1 on A1. Switch on the main switch. The generator oscillates at 2 kHz.
exp3_2_1_s3: Open the generator. Set the modulation to 50 %. The tone is 100 Hz.
exp3_2_1_s4: Look at the curve on the oscilloscope. Trace along the peaks with your finger.
exp3_2_1_h1: You will find the modulation at the bottom of the generator window. At the start it is set to “off”.
exp3_2_1_h2: At 2 ms per square you see two waves of the tone. They contain 40 fast oscillations.
exp3_2_1_loesung: Without modulation the curve is 2 V high everywhere (peak-to-peak). With 50 % it varies between 1 V and 3 V. The peaks form a wave at 100 Hz.
exp3_2_1_erklaerung: The fast oscillation is called the carrier. It carries the tone. The tone changes the height of the carrier. When the tone is up, the carrier gets big. When the tone is down, it gets small. The line over the peaks is called the envelope. It has exactly the shape of the tone. This is called amplitude modulation, AM for short.
exp3_2_1_mehr: For AM, u = Û · (1 + m · sin(2π · f_tone · t)) · sin(2π · f_carrier · t). m is the modulation depth. With m = 50 %, the height varies between half and one and a half times. The RMS value grows only a little, here from 0.71 V to 0.75 V. Medium-wave stations work at about 0.5 to 1.6 MHz. Volta shows you the principle at 2 kHz so you can see every oscillation.
exp3_2_1_w1: Set the modulation to 100 %. What happens at the narrowest points of the curve?
exp3_2_1_w2: Choose a 500 Hz tone. How many waves of the envelope do you see now?
exp3_2_1_echt: A medium-wave station does exactly the same, only much faster: its carrier oscillates about a million times per second. Aircraft radio still uses AM today.
exp3_2_2_frage: Three transmitters arrive at your antenna at the same time. How do you pick out one of them?
exp3_2_2_v1: I need three antennas for that.
exp3_2_2_v2: The tuned circuit only lets through the transmitter it is tuned to.
exp3_2_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_2_2_b1: The display at A5 always stayed the same.
exp3_2_2_b2: At three positions of the variable capacitor the display rose clearly.
exp3_2_2_s1: Plug the antenna coil from C1 to C2 and the variable capacitor from D1 to D2. Connect C1 and D1 to A2, C2 and D2 to 0V. This is your tuned circuit.
exp3_2_2_s2: Plug a 10 pF capacitor from A1 to A2. Put the transmitter station into the desk and connect ANT to A1.
exp3_2_2_s3: Plug the germanium diode from A4 to A5 (ring at A5) and connect A2 to A4. Plug a 22 kΩ resistor from E6 to E7. Connect A5 to E6 and E7 to 0V.
exp3_2_2_s4: Put a voltage display on A5. Tap the variable capacitor and turn it slowly from far left to far right. Watch the display.
exp3_2_2_h1: Turn in small steps. Each transmitter sits on just a narrow stretch.
exp3_2_2_h2: Does the display stay near 0 everywhere? Check that ANT is connected to A1 and that transmitters are on in the transmitter window.
exp3_2_2_loesung: At about 50 pF, 105 pF and 310 pF the display at A5 rises to a few tenths of a volt. These are the transmitters at 1400, 1000 and 600 kHz. In between it stays near 0.
exp3_2_2_erklaerung: The coil and the variable capacitor like to oscillate at one particular frequency. If a transmitter matches it exactly, its oscillation builds up in the circuit. The other transmitters hardly join in. The diode turns the strong oscillation into a voltage you can measure. More capacitance means the circuit oscillates more slowly. That is how you choose the transmitter.
exp3_2_2_mehr: This oscillating along is called resonance. Old radios had a big knob with a scale for it. Behind it sat exactly this kind of variable capacitor.
exp3_2_2_w1: Switch off two transmitters in the transmitter window. Can you still find the third one?
exp3_2_2_w2: Use a 100 pF capacitor instead of 10 pF. Does the circuit still separate the transmitters as well?
exp3_2_2_echt: Old battery radios contain a variable capacitor. Look inside one with an adult – only devices with batteries, never devices with a mains plug.
exp3_2_3_titel: The diode gets the sound out
exp3_2_3_frage: The display at A5 shows how strongly a transmitter arrives. But where is the sound actually hiding?
exp3_2_3_v1: The sound is in the voltage at A5. It wobbles in time with the music.
exp3_2_3_v2: The sound only appears in the loudspeaker.
exp3_2_3_b1: K1 showed a line that wobbles up and down in time with the sound.
exp3_2_3_b3: I couldn't make out anything on the screen.
exp3_2_3_s1: Take your setup from the last experiment. Tune to a transmitter with the variable capacitor.
exp3_2_3_s2: Plug probe K1 onto A5. On the oscilloscope one square lasts 2 milliseconds.
exp3_2_3_s3: Tune to all three transmitters one after the other. Compare the curves.
exp3_2_3_h1: The transmitter oscillates almost a million times a second. That is too fast for the oscilloscope in Volta. It only shows what the diode makes of it.
exp3_2_3_h2: Is the curve too small? Set fewer volts per square on the oscilloscope.
exp3_2_3_loesung: At A5 the voltage wobbles by a few tenths of a volt. That is the sound. With the Morse transmitter you see long and short pieces. With the time signal a short piece comes once a second.
exp3_2_3_erklaerung: The transmitter makes its fast oscillation sometimes stronger, sometimes weaker – in time with the sound. This is called amplitude modulation. The diode only lets through one half of each oscillation. At the resistor the average is left over. It rises and falls in time with the sound. This outline is called the envelope. It is the sound.
exp3_2_3_mehr: Medium wave got its name because the waves are about 200 to 600 metres long. In the past you could hear stations from all over Europe this way – especially far at night.
exp3_2_3_w1: Use a 220 kΩ resistor instead of 22 kΩ. How does the curve change?
exp3_2_3_w2: Switch the transmitters off one by one in the transmitter window. Which curve belongs to which transmitter?
exp3_2_3_echt: A real transmitter needs a licence from the state. That is why the transmitter station only exists here in Volta.
exp3_2_4_frage: A radio with no battery at all – can that work?
exp3_2_4_v1: No. Without a battery there is no sound.
exp3_2_4_v2: Yes. The power comes from the transmitter through the antenna.
exp3_2_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp3_2_4_b1: I heard the transmitter in the crystal earpiece.
exp3_2_4_s1: Take your setup with the tuned circuit and the diode. You don't need a battery.
exp3_2_4_s2: Plug the crystal earpiece from C6 to C7. Connect A5 to C6 and C7 to 0V. The resistor stays next to it.
exp3_2_4_s3: Switch on the app's sound. Turn the variable capacitor until you hear a transmitter.
exp3_2_4_h1: Can't hear anything? Check that the app's sound is on and that the display at A5 is high.
exp3_2_4_h2: The resistor lets the earpiece go again after each wave. Without it the sound is dull and distorted.
exp3_2_4_loesung: With antenna, tuned circuit, diode and crystal earpiece you hear all three transmitters – with no battery at all. All the power comes from the transmitter.
exp3_2_4_erklaerung: The crystal earpiece needs almost no current. The tiny power your antenna catches is enough for it. The tuned circuit chooses the transmitter. The diode gets the sound out. The earpiece makes it audible. A radio like this is called a crystal radio.
exp3_2_4_mehr: The first radios 100 years ago were exactly such crystal radios. Instead of a diode they had a crystal with a fine wire tip. That was the detector.
exp3_2_4_w1: Take the resistor out. How does it sound now?
exp3_2_4_w2: Switch off the transmitter you are listening to in the transmitter window. What do you hear then?
exp3_2_4_echt: You can also build a real crystal radio. Ask an adult to help you. Only string the wire antenna up indoors – never outside, never during a thunderstorm and never near power lines.
exp3_2_5_frage: The crystal earpiece is quiet, and only you can hear it. Can the receiver drive a loudspeaker too?
exp3_2_5_v1: Yes, with a transistor as an amplifier.
exp3_2_5_v2: Yes, you just have to connect the loudspeaker straight to the diode.
exp3_2_5_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_2_5_b1: With the transistor the station could be heard in the loudspeaker.
exp3_2_5_s1: Build the receiver from “Choosing a transmitter”. Tune it to a transmitter.
exp3_2_5_s2: Put in a 10 µF electrolytic capacitor: minus on B6, plus on B7. Connect A5 to B6.
exp3_2_5_s3: Put in transistor T1: base on B8, collector on B9, emitter on C8. Connect B7 to B8 and C8 to 0V.
exp3_2_5_s4: Put a 150 kΩ resistor from E8 to E9. Connect E8 to B8. Take +9V to E10 and connect E9 to E10.
exp3_2_5_s5: Connect E10 to LS1 and LS2 to B9. Switch on the main switch and listen.
exp3_2_5_h1: The loudspeaker sits between +9V and the collector. The 150 kΩ resistor gives the base a small current.
exp3_2_5_h2: Mind the direction of the electrolytic capacitor: plus points towards the transistor.
exp3_2_5_loesung: A quiescent current of about 12 mA flows through the loudspeaker. The sound makes it vary by about 6 mA (peak-to-peak). That is enough to hear the station quietly in the room.
exp3_2_5_erklaerung: The detector supplies only a tiny current. It flows through the electrolytic capacitor into the base of the transistor. In return, the transistor lets a much bigger current flow through the loudspeaker. This current follows every change of the small current, only much more strongly. That is how a quiet sound becomes a loud one.
exp3_2_5_mehr: Here the base current varies by about 0.03 mA. The collector current varies by about 6 mA, roughly 200 times as much. This number is called the current gain β. The electrolytic capacitor lets the sound through but no direct current. So the operating point set by the 150 kΩ resistor stays as it is.
exp3_2_5_w1: Use a 470 kΩ resistor instead of 150 kΩ. Does the sound get much quieter?
exp3_2_5_w2: Measure with the probe at A5 and at B9. Where is the curve bigger?
exp3_2_5_echt: The first pocket radios with transistors came out in the 1950s. They had only a few transistors and played through a small loudspeaker.
exp3_2_6_frage: The 10 pF capacitor couples the antenna only very loosely to the circuit. What happens if the antenna is connected firmly to the circuit?
exp3_2_6_v1: The circuit no longer separates the transmitters. You hear them mixed up.
exp3_2_6_v2: The reception gets louder and separates even better.
exp3_2_6_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_2_6_b1: With 100 nF something arrived even between the transmitters. Turning hardly changed anything any more.
exp3_2_6_b2: With 100 nF the transmitter was louder and separated more sharply.
exp3_2_6_s1: Take your setup from the last experiment. Tune to a transmitter with the variable capacitor.
exp3_2_6_s2: Slowly turn the variable capacitor to between two transmitters. What does the oscilloscope show?
exp3_2_6_s3: Replace capacitor C1 (10 pF) with a 100 nF capacitor.
exp3_2_6_s4: Slowly turn the variable capacitor again. Watch and listen carefully.
exp3_2_6_h1: C1 sits between ANT and the circuit. A big capacitor connects the antenna almost directly to the circuit.
exp3_2_6_h2: At 50 ms per square you can see what the transmitter sends: Morse code, a melody or short beeps.
exp3_2_6_loesung: With 10 pF: on the transmitter about 0.47 V, between the transmitters only about 0.02 V. With 100 nF: about 0.16 to 0.18 V everywhere. The transmitters mix.
exp3_2_6_erklaerung: The antenna has an internal resistance. If it is connected firmly to the circuit, this resistance uses up a lot of energy with every back and forth. The circuit then has a very low quality factor. It hardly prefers its own frequency any more. Then all transmitters get through at the same time. The small capacitor couples the antenna only loosely. That keeps the quality factor high, and the circuit separates the transmitters. This ability is called selectivity.
exp3_2_6_mehr: Here the antenna has 1 kΩ. Connected firmly, it is in parallel with the circuit: Q = R / (2π · f · L) = 1 kΩ / 1.4 kΩ ≈ 0.7. The peak is then about 1.4 MHz wide, wider than the whole range of the three transmitters. With 10 pF the antenna acts like a resistance of about 250 kΩ. Now it is mainly the diode with its 22 kΩ resistor that loads the circuit, like about 11 kΩ. The quality factor rises to about 8.
exp3_2_6_w1: Use a 100 pF capacitor for C1. Is the circuit narrow or wide now?
exp3_2_6_w2: Switch off two transmitters in the transmitter window. Can you now hear the third one at every setting?
exp3_2_6_echt: In real receivers the antenna is often connected to a second, small winding on the coil. That couples it only loosely, and the circuit separates well.
exp3_2_7_frage: The MW module contains a ready-made receiver. What is inside it?
exp3_2_7_v1: The same parts I plugged in myself: coil, diode, transistor and a few more.
exp3_2_7_v2: A completely different part that can only do radio.
exp3_2_7_v3: I don’t know – I’ll take a look.
exp3_2_7_b1: The module contains a coil, a diode, an electrolytic capacitor, resistors and a transistor – like my setup.
exp3_2_7_b2: The module contains one single special part.
exp3_2_7_s1: The MW module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to “+” and “−” to 0V. Connect ANT to “ANT”.
exp3_2_7_s2: Put the variable capacitor from A1 to A2. Connect “Tune” to A1 and A2 to 0V.
exp3_2_7_s3: Take +9V to B1 and from B1 to LS1. Connect LS2 to “out”. Switch on and tune to a transmitter.
exp3_2_7_s4: Tap the magnifier 🔍 on the module (“Look inside”). Compare the parts with your setup from “Louder with an amplifier”.
exp3_2_7_h1: The variable capacitor is not in the module. It sits outside between “Tune” and 0V.
exp3_2_7_h2: The loudspeaker sits between +9V and “out” – like with the transistor in the last experiment.
exp3_2_7_loesung: Inside the module work C_ant with 10 pF, the coil L with 220 µH, the diode D with R_last 22 kΩ, the electrolytic capacitor C_ton, R_b with 150 kΩ and the transistor T1. When tuned, about 12 mA flow through the loudspeaker, with about 6 mA of sound.
exp3_2_7_erklaerung: A module is not a magic box. It packs up a circuit that you understand. The MW module is exactly the receiver you built in this stage. Only the variable capacitor sits outside so that you can tune. That saves you many wires, and you can build the radio into bigger projects.
exp3_2_7_mehr: Real receivers put all the parts on a circuit board or into a single chip. Good medium-wave radios amplify the carrier before the diode and mix it down to a fixed intermediate frequency of 455 kHz. That way they separate the transmitters better than a single circuit.
exp3_2_7_w1: Replace the variable capacitor with a 330 pF capacitor. Which transmitter do you hear now?
exp3_2_7_w2: In “Look inside”, watch T1 while the transmitter is playing and while it is silent. What changes?
exp3_2_7_echt: Medium-wave radios with a handful of transistors used to be in every home. Many still work today – if there is a transmitter nearby.
exp3_2_8_frage: The FM module receives transmitters at about 100 MHz. How do you find a transmitter?
exp3_2_8_v1: I turn the knob P1 slowly until the hiss turns into music.
exp3_2_8_v2: I turn the knob P2. Then every transmitter can be heard.
exp3_2_8_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it out.
exp3_2_8_b1: Between the transmitters it hisses. With P1 I find a transmitter, with P2 I set the volume.
exp3_2_8_b2: With P2 alone I only hear louder hiss.
exp3_2_8_s1: The FM module is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to “+” and “−” to 0V. Connect ANT to “ANT”.
exp3_2_8_s2: Knob P1 becomes the station selector: connect P1a to 0V, P1b to +9V and P1s to “Tune”.
exp3_2_8_s3: Knob P2 becomes the volume: connect P2a to 0V, P2b to +9V and P2s to “Volume”.
exp3_2_8_s4: Connect +9V to LS1 and LS2 to “out”. Switch on. Turn P2 to about three quarters. Then turn P1 slowly until you hear music.
exp3_2_8_h1: Only hiss? Then P1 is between two transmitters. Keep turning very slowly. The music is just below the middle.
exp3_2_8_h2: You hear nothing? Check P2: if it is at zero, the radio is silent. Is “ANT” connected to the antenna?
exp3_2_8_loesung: P1 at about 0.47 tunes to 96.8 MHz, where the melody plays. At 0.09 comes the time signal, at 0.84 Morse code. With P2 at 0.7 the current in the loudspeaker swings by more than 30 mA.
exp3_2_8_erklaerung: P1 divides the battery voltage. This voltage at “Tune” tells the module which frequency to listen to: 0 V is 87.5 MHz, full voltage is 108 MHz. P2 works the same way at “Volume”. So two knobs make a whole radio. Real FM radios often tune with a voltage too.
exp3_2_8_mehr: On medium wave the sound is in the strength of the carrier. This is called amplitude modulation. FM does it differently: the strength stays the same, but the frequency swings a little back and forth in time with the sound. This is called frequency modulation, FM for short. Lightning or a motor mostly disturbs the strength. That is why FM sounds cleaner than medium wave. But FM only reaches about as far as you can see.
exp3_2_8_w1: Look for all three transmitters. At which positions of P1 do you find them?
exp3_2_8_w2: Unplug the wire at “ANT”. What do you hear now?
exp3_2_8_echt: You can solder a real FM radio with a ready-made receiver chip from a kit. Ask an adult who knows about soldering.
exp3_3_1_frage: A voltage regulator turns 9 V into exactly 5 V. Where do the 4 V go that it does not pass on?
exp3_3_1_v1: They turn into heat in the regulator. It gets warm.
exp3_3_1_v2: They flow back into the battery.
exp3_3_1_v3: I don’t know – I’ll measure it.
exp3_3_1_b1: About 4 V drop across the regulator, and it gets much warmer.
exp3_3_1_b3: I don’t see any measured values.
exp3_3_1_s1: Put the voltage regulator on A2, A3 and A4 (IN on A2, GND on A3, OUT on A4). Connect A3 to 0V.
exp3_3_1_s2: Put the current measuring point A between A1 and A2. Connect +9V to A1. This measures the current into the regulator.
exp3_3_1_s3: Put a 150 Ω resistor between A4 and A5. Connect A5 to 0V. This is your load.
exp3_3_1_s4: Put the voltage measuring point V between B2 and B4. Connect A2 to B2 and A4 to B4. Switch on. Watch the temperature below the regulator.
exp3_3_1_h1: The measuring point V measures across the regulator: from IN to OUT, not to 0V.
exp3_3_1_h2: The display works out the power: voltage times current.
exp3_3_1_loesung: About 4 V drop across the regulator. About 37 mA flow into it. That is about 0.15 W. The regulator warms up to about 50 °C.
exp3_3_1_erklaerung: The regulator holds back the current so that exactly 5 V remain at the output. The rest of the voltage drops inside the regulator itself. Voltage times current is power: 4 V times 37 mA is about 0.15 W. This power turns into heat in the regulator. So almost half of the energy from the battery only heats the regulator.
exp3_3_1_mehr: The share of the energy that reaches the load is called efficiency. Here it is about 5 V divided by 9 V, so just over 50 %. The bigger the difference between input and output, the more heat. For large currents a regulator therefore needs a heat sink. Soon you will meet a converter that makes almost no heat.
exp3_3_1_w1: Use 330 Ω instead of 150 Ω. How warm does the regulator get now?
exp3_3_1_w2: Work out the efficiency: the power in the resistor divided by the power from the battery.
exp3_3_1_echt: A plug-in charger that charges a phone for a long time gets warm. In there, too, part of the energy turns into heat. Carefully feel the outside of the case.
exp3_3_2_frage: A regulator holds back the current and gets warm. Can you also dim a lamp by switching it on and off very quickly?
exp3_3_2_v1: Yes. The longer it is on in each cycle, the brighter it shines.
exp3_3_2_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_3_2_b1: The lamp shines steadily. With P1 it gets brighter or dimmer.
exp3_3_2_s1: The 555 is already in the module bar. Connect +9V to + (M8) and to R (M4). Connect − (M1) to 0V.
exp3_3_2_s2: Put the 1 kΩ resistor on A1 and A2. Connect +9V to A1. Connect A2 to DIS (M7) and to the wiper P1s.
exp3_3_2_s3: Put one diode from B1 to B2 (ring towards B2) and a second one from B2 to B3 (ring towards B3). Connect P1a to B1 and B3 to P1b.
exp3_3_2_s4: Put the 1 µF capacitor on B2 and C2. Connect C2 to 0V. Connect B2 to THR (M6) and to TR (M2).
exp3_3_2_s5: Connect the output (M3) to A5. Put the 10 V bulb on A5 and A6 and connect A6 to 0V. Put the probe on C5 and connect A5 to C5. Switch on and turn P1.
exp3_3_2_h1: Nothing lights up? Check the rings of the diodes: both point to the right, from B1 via B2 to B3.
exp3_3_2_h2: On the oscilloscope you see rectangles. Turn P1: the rectangles get wider or narrower, but the rhythm stays the same.
exp3_3_2_loesung: P1 in the middle: the output is on for about half of each cycle. One cycle lasts about 9 ms. That is just over 110 pulses per second. The lamp gets about a third of its rated power. If you turn P1 to the right, it gets brighter.
exp3_3_2_erklaerung: The 555 switches the lamp fully on and fully off more than 100 times per second. That is too fast for the filament: it hardly cools down in the short pause. So the lamp only notices the average. P1 shares the cycle between charging and discharging: turning it makes the on-time longer and the off-time shorter. This ratio is called the duty cycle.
exp3_3_2_mehr: A switch that is fully open or fully closed hardly gets warm: open, no current flows; closed, almost no voltage drops. That is why switching wastes much less energy than braking. This pulse-width modulation, PWM for short, is found in LED lamps, motor controls and chargers.
exp3_3_2_w1: Turn P1 fully to the left and fully to the right. What does the oscilloscope show?
exp3_3_2_w2: Put a 100 µF electrolytic capacitor in place of the capacitor (plus on B2). What do you see at the lamp now?
exp3_3_2_echt: Many LED lamps and bike lights dim with PWM. Film such a lamp in slow motion with a phone: often you see it flicker, although it shines steadily to your eye.
exp3_3_3_frage: An LED sits the wrong way round next to a coil. As long as you press the push button, it stays dark. What happens when you let go?
exp3_3_3_v1: Nothing. Without current from the battery, nothing lights up.
exp3_3_3_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_3_3_b1: When I let go, the LED flashes briefly.
exp3_3_3_b3: The LED lights up as long as I press.
exp3_3_3_s1: Put the push button on A1 and A2 and the 150 Ω resistor on A2 and A3. Connect +9V to A1.
exp3_3_3_s2: Put the 1 H coil on A3 and A5. Connect A5 to 0V.
exp3_3_3_s3: Put the red LED the wrong way round next to the coil: anode on B5, cathode on B3. Connect A3 to B3 and A5 to B5.
exp3_3_3_s4: Put the probe on C3 and connect A3 to C3. Switch on. Press the push button for a while and then let go. Watch the LED and the oscilloscope.
exp3_3_3_h1: The LED must be the wrong way round: its cathode points towards the resistor. Otherwise it already lights up when you press.
exp3_3_3_h2: The flash is short. Look closely when you let go. The pause button stops the oscilloscope.
exp3_3_3_loesung: While pressed, about 36 mA flow through the coil. When you let go, the current keeps flowing for about 10 ms, now through the LED. On the oscilloscope the voltage jumps from +3.6 V to about −2 V.
exp3_3_3_erklaerung: A coil stores energy in its magnetic field. It wants its current to keep flowing. When the push button opens, it drives the current on with a reversed voltage, here through the LED. That is why the LED flashes. Without the LED the current would have no path. Then the voltage would jump to more than a thousand volts.
exp3_3_3_mehr: A diode in this place is called a flyback diode. It catches the switch-off voltage before it does any damage. That is why there is a diode next to every relay and every motor in a transistor circuit. The high voltage can also be useful: the ignition coil in a car makes the sparks for the spark plugs from 12 V this way.
exp3_3_3_w1: Replace the LED with a diode (ring towards B3). How far does the voltage drop now when you let go?
exp3_3_3_w2: Take the LED out completely and let go of the push button. What does the oscilloscope show? Only try this in the app: in real life you would feel an electric shock at the coil.
exp3_3_3_echt: Next to almost every relay on a circuit board there is a small diode. Look at an old relay board together with an adult and find it.
exp3_3_4_frage: A converter turns 9 V into about 5 V. A little over 40 mA then flow through the resistor. How much current does the converter take from the battery for this?
exp3_3_4_v1: More than 40 mA. The converter needs current itself too.
exp3_3_4_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_3_4_b1: Less current comes out of the battery than goes into the resistor.
exp3_3_4_b2: Just as much current comes out of the battery as goes into the resistor.
exp3_3_4_b3: More current comes out of the battery than goes into the resistor.
exp3_3_4_s1: Put measuring point IM1 on A1 and A2 and connect +9V to A1. Put the 470 µF electrolytic capacitor with plus on A2 and minus on A3. Connect A3 to 0V.
exp3_3_4_s2: Build the clock with the 555 as in 3.2: 4.7 kΩ resistor on A2 and B2, two diodes on C1, C2 and C3, 22 nF capacitor on C2 and D2. The 555 gets its current from A2.
exp3_3_4_s3: Connect the 555 output to A4. Put 3.3 kΩ on A4 and A5 and 1 kΩ on A5 and A6. Put the PNP transistor on B5 to C6. Connect A5 to B5, A2 to A6 and A6 to C5.
exp3_3_4_s4: Connect B6 to B7. Put the diode with the ring towards B7: anode on C7, cathode on B7. Put the storage choke on B7 and B8.
exp3_3_4_s5: Put the 100 µF electrolytic capacitor on B8 and C8, measuring point IM2 on B8 and B9 and the 120 Ω resistor on B9 and C9. Put measuring point UM1 on B10 and C10. Connect all minus fields in row C to 0V.
exp3_3_4_s6: Put the probe on A7 and connect it to B7. Switch on. Read all three displays.
exp3_3_4_h1: Does UM1 show almost nothing? Check the PNP transistor: the emitter (E) must go to +9 V after IM1, the base (B) to A5.
exp3_3_4_h2: On the oscilloscope you see a square wave at B7: the transistor switches fully on and fully off. With P1 you change how long it stays on.
exp3_3_4_loesung: UM1 shows about 5.0 V and IM2 about 42 mA. Only about 36 mA come from the battery. In go 9 V · 36 mA = 324 mW, out come 5 V · 42 mA = 210 mW. That is about 65 %.
exp3_3_4_erklaerung: The transistor switches on and off very fast, about 3800 times a second. When it is on, current flows from the battery through the choke. The choke stores energy while doing so. When it is off, the choke drives the current on through the diode, like the coil in 3.3. So the battery only supplies current part of the time. That is why more current comes out than goes in. The energy stays the same: 9 V go in, only 5 V come out.
exp3_3_4_mehr: The voltage regulator from 3.1 would need about 45 mA from the battery for the same load. It turns the rest into heat and only manages about 52 %. The converter manages about 65 %. The rest is used mainly by the 555 itself, the diode and the transistor. With a Schottky diode and a MOSFET, real converters reach over 90 %. They also switch much faster, often a million times a second. Then a tiny choke is enough. Converters like this are inside every phone charger.
exp3_3_4_w1: Turn P1 slowly. How does the voltage at UM1 change? What does the square wave on the oscilloscope do?
exp3_3_4_w2: Work out the efficiency yourself: divide the power that comes out by the power that goes in. Compare it with the voltage regulator from 3.1.
exp3_3_4_echt: Look at the rating label of a USB charger together with an adult. It says what goes in and what comes out. Inside, a switching converter is at work.
exp3_3_5_frage: A white LED needs about 3 V. The cell only has 1.5 V. Can the LED light up anyway?
exp3_3_5_v1: No. The voltage is too small.
exp3_3_5_v2: Yes, if a circuit raises the voltage.
exp3_3_5_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_3_5_b1: The LED lights up. On the oscilloscope the voltage jumps above 3 V.
exp3_3_5_b3: The LED only lights up while I touch the transformer.
exp3_3_5_s1: Set the battery to 1.5 V. Put measuring point IM1 on A1 and A2 and connect +9V to A1. Put the 15 kΩ resistor on A2 and A3.
exp3_3_5_s2: Put the transformer on B2 to C3. The dots point to the left. Connect A2 to B2 and A3 to C3.
exp3_3_5_s3: Put the NPN transistor on B5 to C6. Connect C2 to B5 (base) and B3 to B6 (collector). Connect C5 to 0V.
exp3_3_5_s4: Put the white LED with the anode on B7 and the cathode on C7. Connect B6 to B7 and C7 to 0V. Put the probe on A7 and connect it to B7. Switch on.
exp3_3_5_h1: Nothing lights up? Check the dots on the transformer. If one winding is the wrong way round, the circuit does not oscillate.
exp3_3_5_h2: On the oscilloscope you see short peaks at the collector. They are higher than the 1.5 V of the cell.
exp3_3_5_loesung: The circuit oscillates about 2600 times a second. About 13 mA flow from the cell. At the collector the voltage jumps to just over 3 V, and short pulses of up to 26 mA flow through the LED, about 6 mA on average.
exp3_3_5_erklaerung: The transistor switches on the current through the first winding. The current grows, and the winding stores energy. Meanwhile the second winding gives the transistor base current and keeps it on. When the base current is no longer enough, it switches off suddenly. Now the winding wants to drive its current on, like the coil in 3.3. The voltage rises until the LED conducts. Then everything starts again. This is how the circuit oscillates by itself.
exp3_3_5_mehr: This circuit is called a blocking oscillator. Hobbyists also call it a “joule thief”, because it drains even almost empty cells: it oscillates from about 0.8 V. Real boost converters with a control chip even make 5 V for USB from one cell. The second winding is feedback: the output acts back on the input.
exp3_3_5_w1: Take out the LED and connect it straight to the cell. Does it light up now?
exp3_3_5_w2: Take the LED out completely. What does the oscilloscope show at the collector? Only try this in the app: in real life the high voltage would destroy the transistor.
exp3_3_5_echt: Look for a solar garden light together with an adult. Many have only one 1.2 V cell and still a white LED. Inside there is a small boost converter.
exp3_3_6_frage: The battery only has plus and 0V. Can a circuit make a voltage below 0V from it?
exp3_3_6_v1: No. A battery cannot give less than 0V.
exp3_3_6_v2: Yes, with a clock, capacitors and diodes.
exp3_3_6_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_3_6_b1: UM1 shows about −5.5 V, and the LED lights up.
exp3_3_6_s1: Build the clock with the 555: 1 kΩ on A1 and A2, 4.7 kΩ on A2 and A3, 1 µF capacitor on A3 and B3. Connect +9V to A1, A2 to DIS, A3 to THR and TR, B3 to 0V. The 555 gets plus, reset and minus as always.
exp3_3_6_s2: Connect the 555 output to A5. Put a 100 µF electrolytic capacitor with plus on A5 and minus on A6. Put a diode with the anode on A6 and the cathode on B6. Connect B6 to 0V.
exp3_3_6_s3: Put the second diode with the anode on A7 and the cathode on A6. Put the second electrolytic capacitor with plus on B7 and minus on A7. Connect B6 to B7.
exp3_3_6_s4: Put 1 kΩ on A7 and A8 and the red LED with the anode on B8 and the cathode on A8. Connect B7 to B8. Put UM1 on A9 and B9, connect A7 to A9 and B9 to B8. Connect A6 to the probe on C6. Switch on.
exp3_3_6_h1: Watch the electrolytic capacitors: on the first one, plus points towards the 555; on the second one, plus points towards 0V. The minus leg of the second one really is the minus pole of the new voltage.
exp3_3_6_h2: The LED sits the other way round than usual: the anode goes to 0V. It only lights up if A7 is below 0V.
exp3_3_6_loesung: UM1 shows about −5.5 V, and just under 4 mA flow through the LED. Without the LED it is about −6.4 V. At the probe, A6 jumps in time with the clock between +0.7 V and about −6 V.
exp3_3_6_erklaerung: When the 555 output is high, the first capacitor charges through the first diode. When the output goes to 0V, the charged capacitor pushes its minus side below 0V. Now the second diode conducts and pushes charge into the second capacitor. Cycle by cycle, the circuit pumps charge like this until a minus voltage appears at A7. That is why it is called a charge pump. It stays a little under 9 V, because the 555 and the diodes use up some voltage.
exp3_3_6_mehr: Many circuits need plus and minus, for example operational amplifiers for music. With a charge pump, one battery is enough for this. Charge pumps can also double a voltage. They are inside chips that supply a computer interface with plus and minus voltage. But they are no good for large currents: the capacitors discharge too quickly.
exp3_3_6_w1: Take out the LED. How far down does the voltage at UM1 go now?
exp3_3_6_w2: Replace both electrolytic capacitors with 1 µF capacitors. What happens to the minus voltage when the LED draws current?
exp3_3_6_echt: Ask an adult whether you can find the words “charge pump” in the manual of an old device. They often appear for chips that make −5 V from 5 V.
exp3_3_7_titel: Project: torch with a single cell
exp3_3_7_frage: Your torch should shine brighter than in 3.5. The cell should still last a long time. Can you have both?
exp3_3_7_v1: No. Brighter always means the cell is empty quickly.
exp3_3_7_v2: Yes. With the right resistor there is a good middle way.
exp3_3_7_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_3_7_b1: With 10 kΩ the LED is brighter, and the cell gives just under 20 mA.
exp3_3_7_b2: With 10 kΩ the LED stays dark.
exp3_3_7_b3: With 10 kΩ the circuit draws over 100 mA.
exp3_3_7_s1: Set the battery to 1.5 V. Put IM1 on A1 and A2 and connect +9V to A1. Put a 10 kΩ resistor on A2 and A3. That is less than in 3.5.

exp3_3_7_erklaerung: The cell only stores a certain amount of charge. An AA cell has about 2000 mAh. At 19 mA that is enough for about 100 hours. With 15 kΩ it would be about 150 hours, but the LED is dimmer. With 4.7 kΩ the LED gets brighter, but the cell is empty much sooner. So you have to weigh it up: brightness against running time. Engineers call this a compromise.
exp3_3_7_mehr: The share of the cell’s energy that arrives in the LED is called efficiency. The cell gives about 1.5 V times 19 mA, so about 29 mW. But the LED current flows in pulses, so you have to be careful with average values. The efficiency of such circuits is usually between 50 % and 80 %. The transistor, the resistor and the transformer use up the rest.

lex_thyristor: A thyristor is a switch made of semiconductors. It has an anode A, a cathode K and a gate G. A small current into the gate fires it. Then it conducts from A to K and stays on, even when the gate is free again. It only switches off when the current falls below the holding current of about 3 mA. In the app it only works with low voltage. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.
lex_triac: A triac is like two thyristors connected back to back. That is why it conducts in both directions. Its terminals are called MT1, MT2 and G. A pulse of current into or out of the gate fires it. In every half-wave of the AC voltage it switches off by itself. Only professionals connect dimmers to the mains.
lex_diac: A diac blocks in both directions until the voltage reaches its breakover voltage. Then it breaks over and suddenly conducts well. When the current falls almost to zero, it blocks again. This diac breaks over at 6 V. Diacs for mains dimmers only break over at about 30 V.

exp3_4_1_h1: The button only sends a small current into the gate. The large current for the lamp flows from A to K.
exp3_4_1_h2: Watch the order on the thyristor: A, Gate, K. The gate is in the middle.
exp3_4_1_loesung: After pressing, about 45 mA flow through the lamp. Only just under 2 mA flow into the gate. When you let go, the lamp keeps shining. There are only about 0.8 V between A and K.
exp3_4_1_erklaerung: A thyristor blocks until a current flows into the gate. Then it fires and conducts. After that it keeps itself on: the current from A to K is enough to keep it on. The gate has no say any more. A small pulse of current switches on a large current.
exp3_4_1_mehr: Thyristors switch large currents in machines and railways. A small control current is enough. They used to be in burglar alarms too: a short contact set off the alarm, and it stayed on. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.

exp3_4_2_v1: Not at all. It stays on until the battery is empty.
exp3_4_2_v2: When the current through it gets very small, it goes off.
exp3_4_2_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_4_2_b1: At about 3 mA the current suddenly drops to zero.
exp3_4_2_b2: The current gets smaller, but the thyristor always stays on.
exp3_4_2_b3: The thyristor already goes off when I let go of the button.
exp3_4_2_s1: Turn P1 fully to the left. Put IM1 on A1 and A2 and connect +9V to A1. Put the bulb (10 V) on A2 and A4.
exp3_4_2_s2: Connect A4 to P1 a and P1 s to A6. Put the thyristor on A6 to A8: A on A6, Gate on A7, K on A8. Connect A8 to 0V.
exp3_4_2_s3: Put push button S1 on B1 and B3 and 4.7 kΩ on B3 and B5. Connect +9V to B1 and B5 to A7.
exp3_4_2_s4: Put the second push button S2 on C6 and C8. Connect A6 to C6 and C8 to A8. Switch on and press S1 briefly.
exp3_4_2_h1: Turn P1 to the right very slowly and watch IM1. The lamp goes dark early, but IM1 still shows current.
exp3_4_2_h2: S2 connects A and K directly. Then the current flows past the thyristor.
exp3_4_2_loesung: At the start about 45 mA flow. When you turn P1 up, the current gets smaller. At about 3 mA it suddenly drops to zero: the thyristor is off. If you turn back, it stays off until you press S1. A short press on S2 also switches it off.
exp3_4_2_erklaerung: A thyristor only stays on as long as at least a certain current flows through it. This is the holding current, here about 3 mA. Below that it blocks again. With S2 you take away all its current, because it flows over the button for a moment. After that it blocks, and only a new gate current fires it.
exp3_4_2_mehr: Switching a thyristor off is called commutation. In large systems you switch it off by diverting or reversing the current for a moment. With AC voltage this happens by itself, as you will see in 4.3. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.
exp3_4_2_w1: Press S2 and hold it. Then press S1. What happens when you let go of S2?
exp3_4_2_w2: At which position of P1 does the thyristor go off? Work out how big the resistance is there.
exp3_4_2_echt: Put a battery, a lamp and a push button together with an adult. The lamp only shines while you press. The thyristor in the app, however, remembers being switched on.

exp3_4_3_v2: It goes off by itself, because the voltage keeps returning to zero.
exp3_4_3_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.

exp3_4_3_b2: The lamp keeps shining after letting go.
exp3_4_3_s1: Set the AC source to 9 V~. Connect W~a to A1 and W~b to 0V. Put the bulb (10 V) on A1 and A3.
exp3_4_3_s2: Put the thyristor on A4 to A6: A on A4, Gate on A5, K on A6. Connect A3 to A4 and A6 to W~b.
exp3_4_3_s3: Put the push button on B1 and B3 and 4.7 kΩ on B3 and B5. Connect A1 to B1 and B5 to A5. Put the probe on C4 and connect A4 to C4. Switch on and press the button.
exp3_4_3_h1: Look at the oscilloscope. It shows the voltage at the anode. As long as the thyristor conducts, it is almost zero.
exp3_4_3_h2: In the negative half-wave the anode is below the cathode. Then the thyristor always blocks.
exp3_4_3_loesung: With the button pressed the lamp shines about half as brightly as directly on 9 V~. The thyristor only conducts in the positive half-wave. On the oscilloscope you see: shortly after the start of each positive half-wave the curve drops almost to zero. When you let go, the lamp goes out at once.
exp3_4_3_erklaerung: The AC voltage passes through zero 50 times a second. Then the current falls below the holding current, and the thyristor switches off by itself. In the next positive half-wave the gate must fire it again. That is why it does not stay on with AC voltage. In the negative half-wave it blocks completely.
exp3_4_3_mehr: Because the thyristor only lets one direction through, it is also a rectifier that you can switch on and off. This is how chargers and motors are controlled, for example. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.
exp3_4_3_w1: Put in a 10 kΩ resistor instead of 4.7 kΩ. Where on the curve does the thyristor fire now?
exp3_4_3_w2: And with 22 kΩ? Why does it not fire at all then?
exp3_4_3_echt: Look at a bulb on a battery with an adult. The battery supplies DC voltage, so the lamp shines steadily. Think about it: how many times a second does the voltage of the AC source pass through zero?

exp3_4_4_v1: No. It can only be on or off.
exp3_4_4_v2: Yes. If it fires later in the half-wave, the lamp gets less current.
exp3_4_4_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.

exp3_4_4_b2: P1 changes nothing about the lamp.
exp3_4_4_b3: With P1 the lamp gets brighter than directly on 9 V~.
exp3_4_4_s1: Set the AC source to 9 V~. Connect W~a to A1 and W~b to 0V. Put the bulb (10 V) on A1 and A3 and the thyristor on A4 to A6 (A, Gate, K). Connect A3 to A4 and A6 to W~b.
exp3_4_4_s2: Put 1 kΩ on B1 and B3. Connect A1 to B1, B3 to P1 a and P1 s to B5.
exp3_4_4_s3: Put a 2.2 µF capacitor on B5 and C5 and connect C5 to 0V. Put 1 kΩ on B5 and B7 and connect B7 to A5.
exp3_4_4_s4: Put the probe on C4 and connect A4 to C4. Switch on. Turn P1 slowly and watch the lamp and the oscilloscope. Goal: the lamp shines less brightly than fully to the left.
exp3_4_4_h1: The capacitor charges through P1. The bigger the resistance, the longer it takes until the voltage is enough to fire.
exp3_4_4_h2: Fully to the left the thyristor fires early. Turn P1 a little to the right until the lamp is dimmer.
exp3_4_4_loesung: Fully to the left the lamp shines at about 42 out of 100. With P1 in the middle, about 28 out of 100. On the oscilloscope you see the curve dropping to zero later in each positive half-wave. If you turn further, at some point the thyristor does not fire at all.
exp3_4_4_erklaerung: The capacitor gets its voltage through P1 and 1 kΩ. Its voltage lags behind the AC voltage. Only when it is high enough does enough current flow into the gate. Then the thyristor fires. The bigger the resistance, the later this happens. The lamp only gets the rest of the half-wave. This is called phase control.
exp3_4_4_mehr: With a simple RC network you only get to about the middle of the half-wave. After that the voltage at the capacitor is too small. That is why real dimmers use a diac. You will see this in 4.5. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.
exp3_4_4_w1: Replace the capacitor with a 1 µF one. How far can you dim the lamp now?
exp3_4_4_w2: Set P1 so that the thyristor just no longer fires. Then turn back a little. What do you see on the oscilloscope?
exp3_4_4_echt: Build a lamp with a battery and a push button with an adult. Press the button very quickly again and again. The shorter the lamp is on each time, the dimmer it seems. Phase control works in a similar way, but 50 times a second.
exp3_4_5_frage: The thyristor only uses one half-wave. How does the lamp get the second one too?
exp3_4_5_v1: Not at all. Semiconductors always conduct in one direction only.
exp3_4_5_v2: With a component that can fire in both directions.
exp3_4_5_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_4_5_b1: The lamp shines more brightly than with the thyristor. Both half-waves are cut.
exp3_4_5_b2: The lamp only shines in one half-wave.
exp3_4_5_s1: Set the AC source to 9 V~. Connect W~a to A1 and W~b to 0V. Put the bulb (10 V) on A1 and A3.
exp3_4_5_s2: Put the triac on A4 to A6: MT2 on A4, Gate on A5, MT1 on A6. Connect A3 to A4 and A6 to W~b.
exp3_4_5_s3: Put 4.7 kΩ on B1 and B3 and connect A1 to B1. Put a 0.47 µF capacitor on B3 and C3 and connect C3 to 0V.
exp3_4_5_s4: Put the diac on B3 and B5 and connect B5 to A5. Put the probe on C4 and connect A4 to C4. Switch on.
exp3_4_5_h1: The diac only lets current through when the capacitor reaches 6 V. Then it gives a short pulse of current into the gate.
exp3_4_5_h2: The direction of the diac does not matter. It has no stripe.
exp3_4_5_loesung: The lamp shines at about 60 out of 100. On the oscilloscope you see both half-waves cut: at the top and at the bottom the curve drops to zero after a while. With the thyristor it was at most about 43 out of 100.
exp3_4_5_erklaerung: The triac is like two thyristors connected back to back. It fires in the positive and in the negative half-wave. The diac makes sure the firing is clean: it waits until the capacitor has 6 V and then breaks over. The capacitor discharges into the gate all at once. So the triac fires at the same point in both half-waves.
exp3_4_5_mehr: Triac and diac are in almost every lamp dimmer. But those diacs only break over at about 30 V. The diac in the app breaks over at 6 V already, so that it works on low voltage. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.
exp3_4_5_w1: Put in a 10 kΩ resistor instead of 4.7 kΩ. What happens to the lamp and the curve?
exp3_4_5_w2: Take out the diac and connect B3 directly to A5. Does the triac now fire the same way in both half-waves?
exp3_4_5_echt: Build a bulb on a battery with an adult. Then turn the battery round. The bulb shines equally brightly in both directions, just like the lamp on the triac in both half-waves.

exp3_4_6_frage: Can you build a dimmer that makes the lamp half as bright as directly on 9 V~?
exp3_4_6_v1: No. Half brightness only works with a resistor that gets hot.
exp3_4_6_v2: Yes. Triac and diac simply cut enough off each half-wave.
exp3_4_6_v3: I don’t know – I’ll try it.
exp3_4_6_b1: With P1 I can set the lamp from bright to dark.
exp3_4_6_s1: Set the AC source to 9 V~. Connect W~a to A1 and W~b to 0V. Put the bulb (10 V) on A1 and A3 and the triac on A4 to A6 (MT2, Gate, MT1). Connect A3 to A4 and A6 to W~b.
exp3_4_6_s2: Put 1 kΩ on B1 and B3. Connect A1 to B1, B3 to P1 a and P1 s to B5.
exp3_4_6_s3: Put a 0.47 µF capacitor on B5 and C5 and connect C5 to 0V. Put the diac on B5 and B7 and connect B7 to A5.
exp3_4_6_s4: Put the probe on C4 and connect A4 to C4. Switch on. Goal: the lamp shines at 30 to 50 out of 100. Directly on 9 V~ it would be about 84.
exp3_4_6_h1: Turn P1 to the right, then the triac fires later and the lamp gets dimmer.
exp3_4_6_h2: Look at the oscilloscope: half brightness means that about half of each half-wave is missing.
exp3_4_6_loesung: Fully to the left the lamp shines at about 70 out of 100, fully to the right only at about 25. With P1 at about three quarters it is about 44 out of 100. That is half as bright as directly on 9 V~.
exp3_4_6_erklaerung: Your dimmer cuts a piece off each half-wave. The lamp only gets the rest. Because the triac either blocks completely or conducts completely, it hardly gets warm. A resistor as a dimmer, on the other hand, would produce a lot of heat. That is why dimmers with a triac are so common.
exp3_4_6_mehr: Real dimmers work on the mains with 230 V. That is life-threatening. They also have a choke and a capacitor so that the phase cutting does not send interference into the mains. Only professionals connect devices to the mains.
exp3_4_6_w1: Set the AC source to 6 V~. How does the range in which you can dim change?
exp3_4_6_w2: Replace the capacitor with a 1 µF one. Can you dim the lamp right down to off now?
exp3_4_6_echt: Build a lamp on a battery with an adult and make it dimmer with a variable resistor. Feel whether the variable resistor gets warm. You do not build anything on the mains – only professionals may do that.
